lessons.title: The Three Inputs Behind Every Valuation: Cash Flows, Growth and Risk

children.text: In the last two lessons you met a DCF and a P/E comparison, and saw that they can give very different answers. It is tempting to conclude they are unrelated tools. They are not. Strip away the spreadsheets and the ratios, and every valuation method runs on the same three inputs. Learn to spot those inputs and you can read any valuation, including a broker's one-line target price, and see exactly what it is assuming.

body.text: Every valuation, from a 40-page DCF to a one-line P/E, is a bet on three things: how much cash the business generates, how fast that cash grows, and how risky it is. Methods differ only in where they hide these inputs.

children.text: Input 1: Cash Flows, Not Profits
Shareholders cannot spend accounting profit. They can only benefit from cash the business generates after paying for everything it needs to keep running and growing. That is
free cash flow
, and it can be very different from reported net profit (PAT).

markDefs.definition: Cash from operations minus capital expenditure. It is the cash left over for lenders and shareholders after the business has funded its day-to-day needs and its investment in assets.

children.text: Two fictional companies each report PAT of ₹100 crore. One is an asset-light IT services firm billing large clients monthly. The other is an infrastructure EPC contractor waiting months for payment from state government agencies and constantly buying new equipment.

body.caption: Same profit, very different cash (₹ crore, illustrative)

children.text: The EPC contractor's profit is real on paper, but it is stuck in unpaid bills and new machinery. Year after year, it may need fresh debt or equity just to keep going. Put both companies on the same P/E and you are paying the same price for ₹80 crore of spare cash and for a ₹10 crore hole.

body.text: Watch for a company whose profits rise steadily while cash from operations stays flat or negative for several years. Rising receivables and inventory are the usual culprits. In the worst cases in Indian markets, that gap has been the first visible sign of aggressive accounting.

children.text: Input 2: Growth, and What It Costs
Growth sounds like pure good news. It is not free. To grow, a company must reinvest part of its profit in new plants, stores, working capital or acquisitions. How much it must reinvest depends on its
return on capital employed (ROCE)

markDefs.definition: Operating profit divided by the capital invested in the business (equity plus debt). It measures how much profit each rupee of capital generates. For a company with no debt, it is effectively the same as return on equity.

body.caption: The share of profit a company must reinvest to grow at rate g

children.text: A company earning 30% on capital needs to reinvest only half its profit to grow 15% a year, leaving the other half as free cash flow. A company earning 15% on capital must reinvest all of its profit to grow at the same 15%, leaving nothing for shareholders. Same growth, completely different cash.
Worked example: when growth helps, and when it hurts

Take a fictional debt-free company expected to earn ₹100 crore next year. Investors require a 12% return. Compare four versions of it: one that does not grow at all, and three that grow at 6% a year forever while earning different returns on the capital they reinvest.

body.caption: Value of the same ₹100 crore profit stream at a 12% required return (₹ crore)

cells: 6% growth, returns equal to cost of capital

body.title: Same profit, same growth: value depends on return on capital

content.caption: Value of a cash flow stream growing at g forever, discounted at r

children.text: No growth: ₹100 ÷ 0.12 = ₹833.33 crore.
ROCE 12%: reinvest 6% ÷ 12% = 50%, so FCF = ₹50. Value = ₹50 ÷ 0.06 = ₹833.33 crore.
ROCE 24%: reinvest 6% ÷ 24% = 25%, so FCF = ₹75. Value = ₹75 ÷ 0.06 = ₹1250.00 crore.
This perpetual growth formula is a simplification, and Chapter 3 covers its limits. The relationship it shows holds in full DCF models too.

body.text: Read the chart carefully. Growth at 8% ROCE halved the company's value compared with not growing at all. Growth at exactly 12%, the cost of capital, added nothing. Only growth at 24% created value. Growth creates value only when the return on new capital beats the cost of that capital.

children.text: This is why Indian investors have long paid up for businesses like Asian Paints and Nestlé India, which have for years reported returns on capital well above 25%. Each rupee they reinvest generates far more than investors require. It is also why a company announcing a large capacity expansion should make you ask one question first: what return will this new capital earn?
Input 3: Risk, Expressed as a Required Return
Risk enters a valuation through the
required return

. It starts from what you could earn with almost no risk, which in India is roughly the yield on the 10-year Government of India bond, and adds a premium for everything that could go wrong with the business. Chapter 2 builds this number properly. For now, know what pushes it up.

markDefs.definition: The minimum annual return investors demand to hold a stock, given its risk. In a DCF it is the discount rate. It is also called the cost of equity, or the cost of capital when debt is included.

body.caption: What raises the required return for an Indian stock

cells: Profits swing with commodity prices or the economy: steel, cement, sugar, real estate
High debt relative to operating profit; interest cover below 3 times
A few customers, one product, one state government as the main payer
High promoter share pledging, large related-party transactions, frequent auditor changes
Prices or licences set by government or a regulator
Small-cap stocks with thin trading volumes on NSE and BSE

children.text: Now take the strong-returns company from the example above, still earning 24% on capital and growing at 6%, and change only the required return.

stats.label: Required return 11%
stats.context: Seen as a steady, low-risk business

children.text: Nothing about the cash flows changed. A three percentage point shift in how risky the business is perceived to be moved its value by more than a third. When a stock's price falls sharply on a governance scare with no change in reported earnings, this is the input the market is repricing.
How Multiples Hide the Same Three Inputs
A P/E ratio looks like it skips all of this. It does not. Rearrange the value formula above using return on equity, and you get the P/E a stock deserves based on its fundamentals:

body.caption: Cash conversion and ROE in the numerator, growth and risk in the denominator

children.text: For the strong-returns company, with ROE of 24%, growth of 6% and a 12% required return, the justified forward P/E is 12.5 times. Raise the required return to 14% and it drops to 9.4 times. Cut ROE to 12% and it drops to 8.3 times.

columns.label: Pushes the P/E up
points: Higher return on equity: less reinvestment needed for the same growth
Faster sustainable growth, when ROE is above the required return
Lower risk: a lower required return
Higher cash conversion: profits that turn into cash

columns.label: Pushes the P/E down
points: Slower growth, or growth earned at poor returns
Higher risk: cyclicality, leverage, governance concerns
Profits stuck in receivables, inventory or capex

body.text: The formula shows why real Indian stocks trading at 60 or 80 times earnings are not automatically irrational. Such multiples imply very high growth sustained for a very long time at very high returns on capital, with low risk. The question is never "is 60 times high?" but "do I believe the growth, returns and risk that 60 times requires?"

body.label: Next time someone says a stock "deserves a premium multiple"
body.context: Higher cash conversion, faster growth, better returns on capital or lower risk. If they cannot name one, the premium is a story, not a valuation.

children.text: Where to Find the Three Inputs

cells: Cash flow statement in the annual report, or the Cash Flows section on screener.in
Cumulative CFO vs cumulative PAT over 10 years; capex trend; free cash flow
Compounded sales and profit growth on screener.in; management commentary and capex plans
Sales and profit growth over 3, 5 and 10 years; reinvestment levels
ROCE and ROE history on screener.in
Whether ROCE has stayed above roughly 12 to 15% through a full cycle
Shareholding pattern and pledge data on NSE and BSE; credit ratings from CRISIL, ICRA or CARE; related-party notes in the annual report
Promoter pledging, debt levels, interest cover, rating actions, auditor remarks

body.label: NSE India: company shareholding and corporate filings
body.description: Search any listed company to see its quarterly shareholding pattern, including promoter holding and shares pledged, along with annual reports and exchange announcements.

children.text: Check Your Understanding

body.title: How much cash is left after growth?
body.prompt: A debt-free company earns ₹200 crore of profit and a ROCE of 20%. It wants to grow at 10% a year. How much free cash flow is left for shareholders this year, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Reinvestment rate = growth ÷ ROCE = 10% ÷ 20% = 50%. The company must reinvest ₹100 crore of its ₹200 crore profit, leaving ₹100 crore of free cash flow. At a ROCE of 10%, it would need to reinvest all ₹200 crore to grow at the same rate.

body.title: The capacity expansion
body.question: A listed manufacturer earns a ROCE of 9%. Investors require about 13% from it. Management announces a ₹2,000 crore expansion to double capacity, promising 20% annual revenue growth. Assuming the new plant earns similar returns, what happens to intrinsic value?
options: It rises, because faster growth always increases value
It falls, because the new capital earns less than it costs
It is unchanged, because growth and value are unrelated
It rises, but only if the expansion is funded with debt
body.explanation: Growth creates value only when the return on new capital exceeds the cost of that capital. Here the plant is expected to earn about 9% against a 13% required return, so each rupee invested is worth less than a rupee to shareholders. Faster growth at poor returns destroys value faster.

body.title: The growth rule
body.textWithBlank: Growth creates value only when a company's return on capital is higher than its ___ of capital.
body.explanation: When return on capital equals the cost of capital, growth adds nothing. When it is lower, growth destroys value, as in the 8% ROCE example.

body.title: The fast-growing EPC stock
body.scenario: Aditya, a Delhi-based marketing manager, is excited about a small-cap EPC company on NSE. Its revenue has grown 25% a year for five years and PAT has tripled. On screener.in he also notices: cash flow from operations was negative in four of the last five years, trade receivables have grown faster than revenue, ROCE has averaged 10%, net debt has quadrupled, and promoters have pledged 45% of their shares. The stock trades at 18 times earnings, which a stock tip channel calls "cheap for a 25% grower".
body.prompt: Assess the company on each of the three valuation inputs. Is 18 times earnings cheap?
body.modelAnswer:
Cash flows: poor. Negative operating cash flow in four of five years, with receivables growing faster than revenue, means reported profit is not turning into cash. The "E" in the P/E is of low quality.

Growth: value-destroying as it stands. A 10% ROCE is likely below the company's cost of capital, which for a leveraged small-cap EPC business is probably well above 13%. Growth has been funded by debt, which has quadrupled, and at these returns each rupee of growth reduces value.

Risk: high. Rising debt, dependence on slow-paying clients, small-cap liquidity and 45% promoter pledging all push the required return up. Pledged shares can also be sold by lenders if the price falls, adding to downside risk.

Conclusion: 18 times earnings is not cheap. A multiple only makes sense in light of the three inputs behind it. With weak cash conversion, returns below the cost of capital and high risk, the justified P/E could be well below 18, and possibly not meaningful at all if profits never convert to cash. "Cheap for a 25% grower" ignores what that growth costs and how risky it is.

body.title: A 10-minute three-inputs check on screener.in
steps: Pick any company you own or are considering and open its page on screener.in.
Cash flows: add up cash from operating activities for the last 10 years and compare it with total net profit for the same years. Is it at least 80% of profit?
Cash flows: check capital expenditure in the investing section. How much of operating cash flow does it consume?
Growth: note the compounded sales and profit growth for 5 and 10 years.
Returns: check ROCE for each of the last 10 years. Has it stayed above roughly 12 to 15%, including in weak years?
Risk: check debt to equity, interest coverage, and promoter pledging in the latest shareholding pattern.
Write one sentence on each input. Then look at the P/E and ask whether it matches what you wrote.

points: Every valuation method runs on three inputs: cash flows, growth and risk.
Free cash flow, not profit, is what shareholders ultimately receive. Compare operating cash flow with profit over many years.
Growth costs reinvestment. The reinvestment rate needed is growth divided by return on capital.
Growth creates value only when return on capital exceeds the cost of capital. At or below it, growth adds nothing or destroys value.
Risk enters through the required return. Cyclicality, leverage, concentration, governance and liquidity all push it up and value down.
A P/E multiple hides the same three inputs. A premium multiple must be justified by better cash conversion, faster growth, higher returns or lower risk.

References to Asian Paints and Nestlé India describe historical financial characteristics and are not recommendations.
